cold: Same box, same price, same spot on the shelf.
But open it up and there's less inside.
It's called shrinkflation and it works
because of a tiny bug in how your brain shops.
By the end of this video, you'll know where it hides, why it works so well,
and the one number on the shelf tag that catches it every single time.
ch1: When a company's costs go up, it has two options.
Your $4 box becomes $4.50 and you notice.
Option two, keep it at $4 and put less inside.
Economists call it shrinkflation, shrink plus inflation, and it's not new.
In 2016, Toblerone in the UK widened the gaps between its famous triangles.
The big bar dropped from 400 grams to 360.
ch2: So why does option two work so well?
Because you check prices, you don't check weights.
Researchers studied years of ice cream sales in Chicago.
They found shoppers react about four times more to a
change in price than to the same change in package size.
For a company, that makes the choice easy.
Raise the price and some shoppers walk away,
shrink the package, and most of them never notice.
And the package is built to help.
Same colors, same logo, same size on the shelf.
Often the only thing that changes is one small number on the front, the net weight.
ch3: Once you start looking, you see it everywhere.
In 2022, NPR documented a whole wave of it in the US.
Cottonelle toilet paper, 340 sheets per roll, became 312.
Kleenex, a box of 65 tissues, became 60.
Gatorade started swapping its 32-ounce bottles for 28.
Folgers coffee went from 51 ounces to 43.5,
and the can still said it makes up to 400 cups.
Domino's cut its wing order from 10 pieces to 8 for the same $7.99.
And shrinkflation has a quieter cousin, skimpflation.
Same size, same price, but cheaper ingredients or less service.
That one doesn't even show up on the label.
ch4: For the economy as a whole, shrinkflation is tiny.
Office looked at prices from 2019 to 2024.
Shrinking packages added less than a tenth of one percentage point of that.
So no, it's not why everything feels expensive.
But zoom in on your cart, and it's a different story.
For household paper products, like paper towels,
shrinking packages added three full percentage points of inflation.
And in cereal, only about 1% of products shrank.
But those products made up almost 9% of sales.
In other words, it doesn't hit random items.
It tends to hit the things people buy the most.
ch5: Some governments decided shoppers shouldn't have to play detective.
Since July 2024, large supermarkets in France must put a
notice on products that shrank while the price per unit went up.
Companies that break the rule can be fined up to €15,000.
South Korea now requires companies to disclose it too,
on the package, in the store or online.
And in the US, there's no national rule like that.
Bills have been proposed, but none has passed.
ch6: Remember the one number on the shelf tag that catches it every time?
The small print that tells you what you pay per ounce,
per sheet, or per hundred grams.
The big price can stay frozen for years.
When the package shrinks, the unit price jumps.
Only nine states plus Washington, D.C. require stores to show it.
In most states, it's not required at all.
So if it's there, read it.
If it isn't, do the math on your phone.
One, compare unit prices, not shelf prices.
Two, when a package gets a new design, check the net weight.
Three, count what you actually use.
outro: Shrinkflation works because you're watching the wrong number.
The price on the front is the one they want you to see.
The unit price is the one that tells the truth.
